title: What's really filling your week?
html:
As a weapon engineer in the Royal Navy, I saw experienced senior technicians fall into what I'd call "willy-nilly board shuffling": guessing at a defect and swapping circuit boards until something worked, destroying scarce and expensive parts along the way. More than once I had to supervise the repair of critical equipment myself, and its integration with other systems. The answer was structured fault-finding: find the fault first, then change the part.

Owners treat a heavy week the other way round. The week feels too full, so the fix is more hours, a new app or an early start, before anyone has worked out where the load is coming from. This edition of The Owner's Toolbox is a fifteen-minute fault-finding check for your own week. You'll need your diary for the last fortnight and a pen.

Busy isn't the same as being the constraint

Some weeks are hard because the work is hard: a tender deadline, a factory move, a big customer's first order. That kind of load has a purpose and an end date.

Being the constraint is quieter and lasts longer. Quotes wait for you, questions queue at your door, and decisions you'd normally make in a minute sit for a week. You feel it as overwhelm. The business feels it as lost capacity, and more of your hours rarely fixes it. Nor does delegation fix a business that is simply short of people or machines, so find the cause before you change anything.

The check: twelve statements, four areas

Think about the last fortnight and score each statement 0 (not true), 1 (partly true) or 2 (mostly true).

Workload

  1. There has been more work than fits into the hours I want to work.
  2. My planned work has been broken up by calls, messages or people at the door most days.
  3. A significant change (a new system, site, customer or a key person leaving) has been running on top of normal work.

Control

  1. Decisions that need my attention have been holding up other people's work.
  2. There have been jobs where nobody, me included, was clear who owned them or what "done" meant.
  3. I've spent time on work that someone else could do with the right authority, information or training.
  4. Customers, breakdowns or others have set most of my week before I could plan it.

Motivation and relationships

  1. A working relationship, inside or outside the business, has drained my energy most weeks.
  2. The effort I've put in hasn't come back as progress, recognition or enjoyment.
  3. Much of my time has gone on work that cuts against how I want the business to run.

Mental load and recovery

  1. I've been carrying things in my head rather than on a list or in a system.
  2. Work has followed me home in the evenings or at weekends.

For each area, add the scores and divide by the number of statements, so every area comes out of 2 and they compare fairly. Then look at your single highest-scoring statements too. It's a reflection aid, not a validated questionnaire or a health assessment.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical owner of a 40-person fabrication business. Her scores come out like this:

  • Workload: 1, 2, 0, so 3 ÷ 3 = 1.0
  • Control: 2, 1, 2, 2, so 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75
  • Motivation and relationships: 0, 1, 1, so 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67
  • Mental load and recovery: 1, 2, so 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5

Her instinct was that the problem was workload, because the diary was full. The scores point to control. Her interruptions score of 2 points the same way: most of those calls were people waiting on a decision. Two of her 2s are decisions holding up other people's work and time spent on work someone else could do. When she goes back through the diary, the decision that came back to her most often was approving overtime, which her production manager could handle within a weekly limit.

Mental load scores high too, but some of it comes from the same cause: the overtime approvals she hadn't got to were the ones she was thinking about at home. Fix the control issue and some of that load should ease with it. Check it again when you review.

Before you hand anything over

Three questions decide what stays on your desk.

What's the worst that could happen, both ways? If I hand this over, what's the worst realistic outcome, and could we put it right? If I keep it, what's not getting done instead? A safety-critical decision may well stay with you. Routine overtime within a weekly limit probably doesn't need to.

Does my involvement materially improve the result? Marshall Goldsmith calls the habit "adding too much value": improving someone's work by five per cent while taking away much of their ownership of it.

Is this where my time has the most leverage? The key customers, the big decisions and the people you're developing usually are. Approving overtime usually isn't.

One change this fortnight

Pick one issue. Decide one change, name who owns it and put a review in the diary for two weeks' time. For the owner in the example, that's writing down who now approves overtime, up to what weekly limit, and when it still comes to her.

If your scores point to control too, the first step is the same: take the decision that comes back to you most often and write down who owns it, the limits, and when they should bring it to you. First steps for the other three areas are in the article linked below.

Deal with any urgent safety or business risk straight away, whatever the scores say. If the everyday signs of stress the NHS describes have been there most weeks for a couple of months (poorer sleep, a shorter temper, decisions put off), act now rather than waiting for a quieter quarter, and if it feels heavier than that, talk to your GP.

A template to fill in

  • Highest-scoring area, and its average:
  • My two highest single statements:
  • The one issue I'll change:
  • The change, in one sentence:
  • Who owns it, and their limits:
  • What still comes to me:
  • Review date (two weeks from today):

The printable worksheet is here: https://veterusbusinessgrowth.co.uk/whats-filling-my-week.pdf, and the fuller article on finding the cause is here: https://veterusbusinessgrowth.co.uk/blog/how-to-stop-feeling-overwhelmed-running-an-engineering-business

Repeat the check in 90 days. If the same area keeps coming out on top, the business has probably outgrown how it's organised, and that's hard to see from inside. If you'd like to talk it through, send me a message.

Brad Wright is a Chartered Engineer and former Royal Navy engineer officer who has run large engineering and operations teams in defence, energy and industry. He now advises engineering and technical business owners on improving performance and developing their management teams.
